claim: Reserved Instance discounts do not apply to Spot Instances or to instances running on Dedicated Hosts; for Dedicated Hosts, AWS points to Dedicated Host Reservations.
question: Does a Reserved Instance discount apply to Spot Instances or to instances on a Dedicated Host?

values.display: RIs do not apply to Spot instances
values.spoken: Reserved Instances do not cover Spot or Dedicated Hosts

values.display: purchase Dedicated Host Reservations
values.spoken: for Dedicated Hosts, buy Dedicated Host Reservations

evidence.quote: No, RIs do not apply to Spot instances or instances running on Dedicated Hosts. To lower the cost of using Dedicated Hosts, purchase Dedicated Host Reservations.

claim: A user can stop a running Spot Instance and keep it for later use, but stop is available only for persistent Spot requests.
question: Can a user stop a running Spot Instance, and for which Spot request type?

values.display: Stop is available for persistent Spot requests
values.spoken: you can stop a Spot Instance only with a persistent request

values.display: keep these stopped instances for later use

evidence.quote: Yes, you can “stop” your running Spot Instances when they are not needed and keep these stopped instances for later use, instead of terminating instances or cancelling the Spot request. Stop is available for persistent Spot requests.

claim: A stopped Spot Instance starts only if Spot capacity is still available within the maximum price; capacity is checked at every start.
question: When a user starts a stopped Spot Instance, what decides whether it starts?

values.display: start only if Spot capacity is still available
values.spoken: it starts only if Spot capacity is still there

qualifiers.condition: Spot capacity available within the maximum price

evidence.quote: Note: The Spot Instances will start only if Spot capacity is still available within your maximum price. Spot evaluates capacity availability every time whenever you will start the stopped Spot instances.

claim: A user cannot directly resume a Spot Instance that Spot hibernated; Amazon EC2 controls the hibernate-resume cycle and resumes the instance when capacity becomes available.
question: Can a user resume a Spot Instance that was hibernated on interruption?

values.display: Hibernate-resume cycle is controlled by Amazon EC2
values.spoken: Amazon EC2, not you, resumes it

values.display: when the capacity becomes available

evidence.quote: No, you will not be able to resume a hibernated instance directly. Hibernate-resume cycle is controlled by Amazon EC2. If an instance is hibernated by Spot, it will be resumed by Amazon EC2 when the capacity becomes available.

claim: On interruption a Spot Instance can be terminated, stopped or hibernated; stop and hibernate need a persistent Spot request or a Spot Fleet with the maintain option, and by default the instance is terminated.
question: What happens to a Spot Instance when it is interrupted, and what is the default?

values.display: By default, your instances are terminated
values.spoken: by default an interrupted Spot Instance is terminated

values.display: terminated, stopped or hibernated upon interruption

qualifiers.condition: stop and hibernate only for persistent Spot requests and Spot Fleets with maintain

evidence.quote: You can choose to have your Spot instances terminated, stopped or hibernated upon interruption. Stop and hibernate options are available for persistent Spot requests and Spot Fleets with the “maintain” option enabled. By default, your instances are terminated.

claim: Amazon EC2 reclaims a Spot Instance for two possible reasons: mainly its own capacity requirements, or a Spot price that rises above the maximum Spot price the user chose to set.
question: Why would Amazon EC2 interrupt a Spot Instance?

values.display: Amazon EC2 capacity requirements
values.spoken: mostly because EC2 needs the capacity back

values.display: the Spot price rises above this
values.spoken: or the Spot price goes above your maximum price

qualifiers.scope: Spot Instance interruptions by Amazon EC2
qualifiers.condition: the price reason applies only when a maximum Spot price is set

evidence.quote: In the circumstance EC2 needs to reclaim your Spot Instance it can be for two possible reasons, with the primary one being Amazon EC2 capacity requirements (e.g. On Demand or Reserved Instance usage). Alternatively, if you have chosen to set a “maximum Spot price” and the Spot price rises above this, your instance will be reclaimed with a two-minute notification.

claim: The maximum Spot price is set to the On-Demand price by default, and a running Spot Instance pays the Spot market price, not the maximum price, in per-second increments.
question: What is the default maximum Spot price, and which price does a running Spot Instance pay?

values.display: is set at the On-Demand price
values.spoken: the maximum price defaults to the On-Demand price

values.display: pay the Spot market price
values.spoken: you pay the Spot price, not your maximum

qualifiers.scope: Spot Instances, maximum Spot price parameter

evidence.quote: This parameter determines the maximum price you would be willing to pay for a Spot instance hour, and by default, is set at the On-Demand price. As before, you continue to pay the Spot market price, not your maximum price, at the time your instance was running, charged in per-second increments.

claim: Over the last 3 months, 92% of Spot Instance interruptions were customers terminating the instance themselves because the application had completed its work.
question: According to the EC2 FAQ, what causes most Spot Instance interruptions?

values.spoken: ninety-two percent

qualifiers.scope: Spot Instance interruptions over the last 3 months, as stated by the FAQ

evidence.quote: Over the last 3 months, 92% of Spot Instance interruptions were from a customer manually terminating the instance because the application had completed its work.

claim: A Spot capacity pool is a set of unused EC2 instances with the same instance type, operating system and Availability Zone, and each pool can have a different price.
question: What is a Spot capacity pool?

values.display: same instance type, operating system, and Availability Zone
values.spoken: unused instances of one type, one OS, one zone

values.display: can have a different price

evidence.quote: A Spot capacity pool is a set of unused EC2 instances with the same instance type, operating system, and Availability Zone. Each spot capacity pool can have a different price based on supply and demand.

claim: AWS recommends using multiple Spot capacity pools to get the most Spot capacity, and EC2 Auto Scaling, EC2 Fleet and Spot Fleet can find cost-effective capacity across pools.
question: What is the main Spot best practice in the EC2 FAQ?

values.display: using multiple Spot capacity pools
values.spoken: spread Spot across many capacity pools

evidence.quote: We highly recommend using multiple Spot capacity pools to maximize the amount of Spot capacity available to you. EC2 provides built-in automation to find the most cost-effective capacity across multiple Spot capacity pools using EC2 Auto Scaling, EC2 Fleet or Spot Fleet.

claim: If Amazon EC2 terminates or stops a Spot Instance in its first instance hour, that usage is not charged; if the user stops or terminates it, usage is charged to the nearest second.
question: How is a Spot Instance charged when Amazon EC2 interrupts it in the first hour, compared with when the user stops it?

values.display: you will not be charged for that usage
values.spoken: interrupted by EC2 in the first hour: no charge

values.display: charged to the nearest second
values.spoken: stopped by you: charged per second

qualifiers.scope: Spot Instance billing on stop or interruption
qualifiers.condition: the free first hour applies only when Amazon EC2 stops or terminates the instance

evidence.quote: If your Spot instance is terminated or stopped by Amazon EC2 in the first instance hour, you will not be charged for that usage. However, if you stop or terminate the Spot instance yourself, you will be charged to the nearest second.

claim: While running, Spot Instances are the same as On-Demand or Reserved Instances; Spot is best suited for fault-tolerant, flexible workloads.
question: Is a running Spot Instance different from an On-Demand Instance, and which workloads suit Spot?

values.display: exactly the same as On-Demand or Reserved instances
values.spoken: a running Spot Instance is the same instance

values.display: best suited for fault-tolerant, flexible workloads
values.spoken: use Spot for fault-tolerant, flexible work

evidence.quote: While running, Spot Instances are exactly the same as On-Demand or Reserved instances.
Spot uses the same underlying EC2 instances as On-Demand and Reserved Instances, and is best suited for fault-tolerant, flexible workloads.

claim: A Spot Instance pays the Spot price in effect at the beginning of each UTC hour, applied to the usage of the following hour.
question: Which Spot price does a running Spot Instance pay when the price changes?

values.display: beginning of each UTC hour
values.spoken: the price at the start of each UTC hour

evidence.quote: You pay the Spot price in effect at the beginning of each UTC hour. The Spot price for your running instance is evaluated at the beginning of every UTC hour (e.g., 09:00:00 UTC, 12:00:00 UTC, etc) and applied to your instance’s usage for the subsequent hour.

claim: Linux/UNIX, Windows Server and Red Hat Enterprise Linux are available as Spot Instances; Windows Server with SQL Server is not currently available.
question: Which operating systems can run as Spot Instances?

values.display: Windows Server with SQL Server
values.spoken: Windows with SQL Server is not available on Spot

evidence.quote: Linux/UNIX, Windows Server and Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) are available. Windows Server with SQL Server is not currently available.

claim: EC2 Fleet does not fail over to On-Demand when Spot capacity is not fully available; it keeps trying to meet the requested Spot capacity.
question: Will an EC2 Fleet fall back to On-Demand if Spot capacity is not fully available?

values.display: attempt to meet your desired Spot capacity
values.spoken: no, it keeps trying to get Spot

evidence.quote: No, EC2 Fleet will continue to attempt to meet your desired Spot capacity based on the number of Spot instances you requested in your Fleet launch specification.

claim: An EC2 Fleet request cannot span multiple Regions; multi-Region EC2 Fleet requests are not supported.

values.display: do not support multi-region EC2 Fleet requests
values.spoken: an EC2 Fleet is one Region only

evidence.quote: No, we do not support multi-region EC2 Fleet requests.

claim: An On-Demand Instance launched by EC2 Fleet that matches an existing Reserved Instance receives the Reserved Instance discount.

qualifiers.condition: the instance matches an existing Reserved Instance

claim: Spot Fleet requests are not guaranteed to be fulfilled; they are subject to the same availability and prices as a single Spot Instance request.

values.display: subject to the same availability and prices
values.spoken: no, Spot Fleet has the same availability as one Spot request

evidence.quote: Spot fleet requests allow you to place multiple Spot Instance requests simultaneously, and are subject to the same availability and prices as a single Spot Instance request.

claim: Savings Plans do not reserve capacity; capacity can be reserved with On-Demand Capacity Reservations, which Savings Plans can make cheaper.

values.display: Savings Plans do not provide a capacity reservation
values.spoken: Savings Plans give a discount, not capacity

values.display: pay lower prices on them with Savings Plans

evidence.quote: No, Savings Plans do not provide a capacity reservation. You can however reserve capacity with On-Demand Capacity Reservations and pay lower prices on them with Savings Plans.

claim: Capacity Blocks give scheduled, future-dated GPU capacity for ML workloads, while On-Demand Capacity Reservations give immediate, flexible capacity assurance for any workload with no advance scheduling or fixed end date.
question: When should Capacity Blocks be used instead of On-Demand Capacity Reservations?

values.display: scheduled, future-dated GPU capacity specifically for ML workloads
values.spoken: Capacity Blocks: GPU capacity for ML on future dates

values.display: flexible, immediate capacity assurance for any workload
values.spoken: Capacity Reservations: capacity now, any workload

evidence.quote: The key difference is that Capacity Blocks provide scheduled, future-dated GPU capacity specifically for ML workloads, while On-Demand Capacity Reservations offer flexible, immediate capacity assurance for any workload without requiring advance scheduling or a fixed end date.

claim: A Capacity Block can be purchased as far out as eight weeks into the future, or for now when capacity is available.

values.spoken: up to eight weeks ahead

values.display: one to 64 instances
values.spoken: one to sixty-four instances

evidence.quote: With Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks, you can reserve GPU capacity starting on a future date for durations up to 6 months and in cluster sizes of one to 64 instances.

values.spoken: no changes and no cancel after you reserve it

values.display: not covered by Savings Plans or RI discounts

values.spoken: paid up front

You can view the price of an EC2 Capacity Block offering before you reserve it, and the price of an EC2 Capacity Block is charged up front at the time the reservation is made.
